title: the summit sit
hook: a song closes by saying whose it is: the women who signed their own names, and the names they signed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit listened to the women of the epics: Sita arguing, Gandhari refusing to flatter, Savitri talking with Death. Did you ask what a woman in a story actually said? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHAT DID SHE ACTUALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain. That phrase closes song after song sung in Mirabai's name, like a stamp pressed into wax. Singers call it a chhap. Yesterday's women were given their words by the poets of the epics. The next stretch of the year was different. It turned to women whose own words survive, in songs and in a few lines of scripture, sometimes with their names pressed right into them. Today's summit sit goes back to those signatures.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR.` → `A STAMP PRESSED INTO WAX.` → `WOMEN IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the names they gave their God. Mira's songs end on Giridhar. Akka Mahadevi, in Karnataka, closes her vachanas on the lord white as jasmine. Andal, in Tamil, dreams her whole wedding to the Lord, verse by verse, each one ending, I dreamed it, friend. A name for God, chosen and repeated, becomes a way of knowing whose voice you're hearing. Then the names they gave themselves. Karaikkal Ammaiyar's tradition says Shiva called her Mother. But in her own hymns she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground, dancing near him in the night. She didn't hide the bones. She signed with them. Lal Ded, in Kashmir, let people curse her and let others bring her flowers, and said neither one could touch her. And some of these women left no songs at all, only questions, kept in an Upanishad. Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, layer after layer, and when she's told to stop, she comes back later with two more questions, like a warrior stringing a bow. Maitreyi, offered a share of property, asks what she would do with something that can't make her immortal. Without her question, the teaching that follows has no door. Now one honest turn. With songs that traveled mouth to mouth, nobody can always say which lines go back to the woman herself. Some readers sort older from newer. Others say a song stays alive by being sung and changing a little in every mouth. Either way, the signature keeps doing its work. Whoever sings the song steps aside at the end: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord.
screen: `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEIR GOD.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEMSELVES.` · `GARGI AND MAITREYI: THE QUESTIONS.` · `THE SINGER STEPS ASIDE.` · then, large: `NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a name at the end. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one of these voices: Mira, Akka, Andal, Lal Ded, Gargi, Maitreyi, Karaikkal Ammaiyar. Let her signature stand in the quiet for a moment. Then notice: at the end of this breath, and the next, whose name rises in you? A person's, a place's, or no name at all. Let it come, and let it go with the out-breath. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you already use. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women in their own words, and the names they signed. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, when you sign your name, on a form, a card, a message, let it be a small chhap, and notice whose words you're carrying. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: The songs of women saints such as Mirabai, Andal and Akka Mahadevi are still sung in homes, temples and gatherings, and some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's wedding song at their own weddings.

fork.setup: you're Mirabai in Vrindavan. you ask to meet a holy man, and word comes back: he has vowed not to see women. what do you send back?
options: an angry letter about his vow.
one sentence: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna.
fork.reveal: in the story, Mira says she thought Krishna was the only man in Vrindavan, and the renunciant comes out to meet her. it's told about her, not recorded at the door.

original.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: chhāp, a stamp, the closing name that tells you whose song it is.

trapdoor: what you thought: the women saints' songs are anonymous folk songs.
what it means: many carry a signature, a name for God or for the singer, pressed into the last line.

what a scholar hears: the chhap or signature line, like Mira's Giridhar and Akka's lord white as jasmine, marks a voice and a lineage, while which lines go back to the saint herself is still discussed.

sources.ref: Songs attributed to Mirabai (the closing line 'Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar')
Vachanas of Akka Mahadevi (the signature 'lord white as jasmine', Chennamallikarjuna)
Karaikkal Ammaiyar, Tiruvalankattu Mutta Tiruppatikam (closing signature); Periya Puranam (her life)
Lal Ded's vakh on praise and blame

notes: Summit sit, revisiting the poet-saints and 'in their own words where they exist' (1353–1369). Recaps follow the year's own scripts: Mirabai 1357–1358, Akka 1362, Andal 1355, Lal Ded 1365, Gargi 1367, Maitreyi 1368, Karaikkal Ammaiyar 1369.
The opening line 'Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar' is a transliteration, not an English translation; it is the signature line as given on 1358. Confirm transliteration.
Akka's 'lord white as jasmine' (Chennamallikarjuna) described as the name that closes her vachanas; confirm 'closes' is fair for her ankita.
Karaikkal Ammaiyar's signature as the pey of Karaikkal follows 1369; the specific patikam named in sources should be confirmed.
The fork's Mira and the renunciant is a story told about her (1357), not a recorded event; the reveal says so. The renunciant is sometimes named as Jiva Goswami; not named here.
Original: छाप (chhāp), Hindi; confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
Editor pass: myth explanation corrected: in BU 3.8 Gargi herself uses the warrior-and-bow image, not the narrator.
